stem: Labyrinthitis is best defined as which of the following?
options: An inner ear disorder characterized by inflammation or infection of the labyrinth, a structure responsible for balance and hearing
An outer ear disorder characterized by infection of the pinna
A disorder of the optic nerve affecting visual acuity
A disorder of the oral mucosa affecting taste perception

stem: Among infectious causes of labyrinthitis, which category is described as MOST common?
options: Viral causes, such as herpes simplex, influenza, measles, and mumps
Bacterial causes spread from otitis media
Fungal causes from Candida species
Parasitic causes from intestinal helminths

stem: Bacterial labyrinthitis typically arises from spread of infection from which conditions?
options: Otitis media or meningitis
Appendicitis or cholecystitis
Urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis
Peptic ulcer disease or gastritis

stem: Besides infectious causes, which non-infectious causes of labyrinthitis are specifically listed?
options: Autoimmune conditions and allergic reactions
Chronic kidney disease and nephrotic syndrome
Osteoarthritis and gout
Peripheral vascular disease and varicose veins

stem: The pathophysiology of labyrinthitis describes disruption of the normal function of which two systems?
options: The cochlea (hearing) and the vestibular system (balance)
The retina (vision) and the optic nerve
The olfactory bulb (smell) and the trigeminal nerve
The tongue (taste) and the facial nerve

stem: In the pathophysiology of labyrinthitis, which triggering events are described as leading to inflammation?
options: Direct viral or bacterial invasion of the labyrinth, or autoimmune/allergic immune responses
Only mechanical trauma from a blow to the head
Only prolonged exposure to loud noise
Only congenital malformation of the cochlea

stem: Inflammation in labyrinthitis affects which specific inner ear structures?
options: The semicircular canals, utricle, saccule, and cochlea
The tympanic membrane and ossicles only
The pinna and external auditory canal only
The eustachian tube only

stem: Inflammation of the labyrinth leads to which immediate physiological changes?
options: Swelling, increased fluid production, and disruption of normal function
Immediate and permanent calcification of the cochlea
A sudden, isolated increase in taste sensitivity
A compensatory increase in visual acuity

stem: In the disruption of vestibular function seen in labyrinthitis, what causes symptoms such as vertigo, imbalance, and nystagmus?
options: A mismatch between vestibular signals, visual input, and proprioception
A complete and isolated loss of the sense of smell
An isolated increase in blood pressure with no sensory component
A purely psychological reaction with no physiological basis

stem: Inflammation of the cochlea in labyrinthitis interferes with auditory signal transmission, resulting in which findings?
options: Hearing loss (usually unilateral) and tinnitus
Bilateral loss of the sense of taste
Complete, permanent loss of the sense of touch
An isolated increase in hearing sensitivity with no other change

stem: Inflammatory mediators and fluid buildup in labyrinthitis irritate which cranial nerve?
options: Cranial nerve VIII (the vestibulocochlear nerve)
Cranial nerve II (the optic nerve)
Cranial nerve VII (the facial nerve) exclusively, with no effect on hearing or balance
Cranial nerve X (the vagus nerve)

stem: What may happen if the inflammation of labyrinthitis resolves appropriately?
options: Normal function may return
Permanent, irreversible deafness always occurs regardless of resolution
The patient will always develop chronic bacterial meningitis
Vision will permanently improve beyond baseline

stem: Prolonged or severe inflammation, particularly in bacterial labyrinthitis, can lead to which outcome?
options: Permanent hearing loss or vestibular dysfunction
A guaranteed full recovery within 24 hours in every case
Spontaneous resolution with no risk of any lasting effect
Improved baseline hearing compared to before the illness

stem: The severe vertigo of labyrinthitis is typically described with which onset and duration pattern?
options: Often sudden onset, lasting hours to days
Always gradual onset over several years
Lasting only a few seconds with no further recurrence ever
Present continuously and unchanged for decades before diagnosis

stem: Besides severe vertigo, which gastrointestinal symptoms are commonly associated with labyrinthitis?
options: Nausea and vomiting
Chronic constipation unrelated to vertigo
Bloody diarrhea with abdominal cramping
Dysphagia to solids only, with no vertigo-related symptoms

stem: Besides nausea, vomiting, and vertigo, which additional vestibular symptom is listed for labyrinthitis?
options: Loss of balance or unsteadiness
Sudden, isolated weight gain
Chronic, isolated joint pain in the knees
Progressive loss of the sense of smell

stem: Auditory symptoms of labyrinthitis include hearing loss and which other finding?
options: Tinnitus (ringing in the ears)
Complete, isolated loss of taste
Persistent nasal congestion with no ear involvement
Chronic dry eyes with no auditory symptoms

stem: Fever, as an associated symptom of labyrinthitis, is typically seen in which circumstance?
options: If the cause is infectious
Only in purely autoimmune cases with no infection
Only in cases caused by allergic reactions, never infection
Only after full recovery, never during active illness

stem: Headache, as an associated symptom of labyrinthitis, is typically related to which underlying process?
options: A systemic infection
A completely unrelated dental abscess
A chronic skin condition with no systemic involvement
A pre-existing visual refractive error only

stem: In the diagnostic clinical history for labyrinthitis, which features are typically sought?
options: Recent viral or bacterial infection, with sudden onset of vertigo and hearing loss
A decades-long history of gradually progressive joint stiffness only
A family history of a single, unrelated skin condition only
A history of chronic, stable visual impairment since childhood only

stem: During physical examination for suspected labyrinthitis, the head impulse test is used to assess for which finding?
options: Abnormal eye movements indicating vestibular dysfunction
Abnormal reflexes in the lower limbs only
Abnormal pupillary constriction to light only
Abnormal skin turgor indicating dehydration only

stem: Besides the head impulse test, which other physical examination component is used in suspected labyrinthitis?
options: Gait and balance tests
Fundoscopic examination of the retina only
Palpation of the abdomen for organomegaly only
Auscultation of bowel sounds only

stem: Audiometry is used in the special testing of labyrinthitis to assess which parameter?
options: Hearing loss
Visual acuity
Blood glucose level
Renal function

stem: Which vestibular function tests are specifically listed for the special testing of labyrinthitis?
options: Caloric testing and videonystagmography
Spirometry and peak flow measurement
Electrocardiography and echocardiography
Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy

stem: Imaging studies such as MRI or CT are used in the workup of labyrinthitis primarily to exclude which other conditions?
options: Acoustic neuroma or stroke
A simple, uncomplicated common cold
A minor, superficial skin abrasion
A routine dental cavity

stem: Which differential diagnosis for labyrinthitis is specifically characterized by vertigo WITHOUT hearing loss?
options: Vestibular neuritis
Meniere's disease
Acoustic neuroma
Bacterial labyrinthitis

stem: Which differential diagnosis for labyrinthitis is characterized by episodic vertigo, hearing loss, AND tinnitus together?
options: Meniere's disease
Vestibular neuritis
A simple tension headache
Uncomplicated otitis externa

stem: Besides vestibular neuritis and Meniere's disease, which other conditions are listed in the differential diagnosis of labyrinthitis?
options: Acoustic neuroma, and stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA)
Appendicitis and cholecystitis only
Peptic ulcer disease and pancreatitis only
Gout and rheumatoid arthritis only

stem: Which supportive care measures are recommended for the general management of labyrinthitis?
options: Bed rest and hydration
Strenuous aerobic exercise and fluid restriction
Complete fasting and strict bed confinement with no fluids at all
Prolonged standing exercises in bright, flashing light

stem: In the acute phase of medical therapy for labyrinthitis, which class of medication is used specifically for inflammation?
options: Corticosteroids, such as prednisone
Insulin
Loop diuretics
Anticoagulants

stem: Antiviral drugs are indicated in the management of labyrinthitis under which circumstance?
options: If a viral cause is suspected
In every single case regardless of suspected cause
Only for cases with no vertigo at all
Only after complete resolution of all symptoms

stem: Antibiotics are indicated in the management of labyrinthitis under which circumstance?
options: If bacterial infection is confirmed
In every single case regardless of suspected cause
Only for purely autoimmune labyrinthitis
Only for allergic labyrinthitis

stem: Which medication class, such as promethazine, is used for symptomatic relief of nausea in labyrinthitis?
options: Antiemetics
Antihypertensives
Anticoagulants
Bronchodilators

stem: Which medication class, such as meclizine or benzodiazepines, is used to manage vertigo in labyrinthitis?
options: Vestibular suppressants
Loop diuretics
Proton pump inhibitors
Antifungal agents

stem: What is the purpose of vestibular rehabilitation therapy (VRT) in the management of labyrinthitis?
options: Exercises to restore balance
Surgical removal of the inflamed labyrinth in every case
Permanent avoidance of all physical activity indefinitely
Replacement of the need for any medical therapy

stem: Hearing aids are indicated in the management of labyrinthitis for which specific situation?
options: Persistent hearing loss
Acute vertigo occurring without any hearing involvement
Fever occurring without any auditory symptoms
Nausea occurring without any auditory symptoms

stem: What is the typical prognosis for VIRAL labyrinthitis, in terms of recovery?
options: Recovery is typically complete, but may take weeks to months
Recovery never occurs under any circumstances
Recovery is always instantaneous, within minutes of symptom onset
Recovery is impossible without surgical intervention in every case

stem: What is the prognosis concern specifically associated with BACTERIAL labyrinthitis if not treated promptly?
options: It may lead to permanent hearing loss or balance issues
It always resolves spontaneously without any treatment or consequence
It has no risk of any lasting complication under any circumstance
It exclusively affects taste, never hearing or balance

stem: Which of the following is listed as a potential complication of labyrinthitis affecting balance long-term?
options: Chronic imbalance
Permanent loss of the sense of smell
Chronic constipation
Permanent loss of taste on the tongue

stem: Besides chronic imbalance and persistent hearing loss, which psychological complication is listed for labyrinthitis?
options: Anxiety or depression from prolonged symptoms
Permanent, isolated loss of short-term memory only
A specific phobia of heights only
Obsessive-compulsive disorder exclusively

stem: Which vaccination is specifically listed as a preventive measure against labyrinthitis, by preventing mumps?
options: The MMR vaccine
The tetanus vaccine
The yellow fever vaccine
The oral polio vaccine

stem: Besides vaccination, which other measure is listed for the prevention of labyrinthitis?
options: Prompt treatment of otitis media and upper respiratory infections
Avoidance of all forms of physical exercise indefinitely
Routine use of antibiotics in every healthy individual regardless of infection
Avoidance of all dietary protein intake

stem: For patients with a suspected allergic trigger, which preventive measure is recommended for labyrinthitis?
options: Avoidance of known allergens
Daily high-dose antihistamine use regardless of allergen exposure
Complete avoidance of all fluid intake
Permanent bed rest regardless of symptom status

stem: In the nursing assessment of a patient with labyrinthitis, which vital sign findings should specifically be monitored?
options: Fever, hypotension, or signs of dehydration
Only the patient's pupillary response to light
Only the patient's deep tendon reflexes
Only the patient's skin color on the lower extremities

stem: Besides vital signs, nursing assessment of labyrinthitis should evaluate the severity and duration of which specific symptoms?
options: Vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus
Joint swelling and morning stiffness
Skin rash distribution and pruritus
Urinary frequency and dysuria

stem: Why should the nurse closely evaluate the intensity of nausea and vomiting in a patient with labyrinthitis?
options: To prevent dehydration
Because nausea and vomiting in labyrinthitis have no clinical significance
Because nausea and vomiting always indicate an unrelated gastrointestinal infection requiring separate treatment
Because nausea and vomiting are the only symptoms that ever require nursing documentation

stem: Besides physical symptoms, nursing assessment of labyrinthitis should also observe for signs of which psychological state?
options: Anxiety or distress due to vertigo and sensory changes
Excessive euphoria with no other mood change
Complete absence of any emotional response in all patients
Overconfidence in balance abilities during acute vertigo

stem: Reviewing the patient's medical history in labyrinthitis assessment should specifically include which information?
options: Recent infections or ear conditions
Only the patient's childhood vaccination record for unrelated illnesses
Only the patient's dental history
Only the patient's family history of unrelated skin conditions

stem: During the acute phase of labyrinthitis, why should the patient be encouraged to remain in bed during severe vertigo episodes?
options: To avoid falls
Because bed rest cures the underlying infection without any further treatment
Because standing permanently worsens hearing regardless of vertigo status
Because bed rest eliminates the need for any medication

stem: As part of creating a safe environment for a patient with acute labyrinthitis, what should the nurse do regarding the patient's surroundings?
options: Remove obstacles and ensure a clutter-free environment
Rearrange furniture frequently to keep the patient alert
Encourage the patient to walk in a dimly lit, obstacle-filled hallway unassisted
Leave all mobility aids out of reach to encourage independence prematurely

stem: Why should the nurse assist with mobility, especially during episodes of dizziness, in a patient with labyrinthitis?
options: To reduce the risk of falls during unsteady movement
Because mobility assistance has no effect on fall risk in labyrinthitis
Because the patient should always be left to mobilize completely unsupervised during acute vertigo
Because mobility assistance is only relevant after full recovery, never during acute symptoms

stem: Promoting rest and comfort for a patient with acute labyrinthitis includes which environmental intervention?
options: Positioning the patient in a quiet, darkened room to reduce stimuli
Positioning the patient near bright, flashing lights to stimulate alertness
Encouraging loud background music to distract from vertigo
Encouraging frequent rapid head turning to 'test' the vestibular system

stem: Encouraging the use of a supportive pillow in acute labyrinthitis care serves which specific purpose?
options: To keep the head stable
To increase neck flexibility through frequent stretching
To elevate the feet above the level of the heart for venous return
To replace the need for any vestibular suppressant medication

stem: Ensuring hydration in the nursing management of labyrinthitis includes monitoring which parameter?
options: Fluid intake and output
Only the patient's dietary fiber intake
Only the patient's daily step count
Only the patient's screen time

stem: In the subacute phase of labyrinthitis recovery, how should mobility be approached?
options: Mobility should be encouraged as tolerated, gradually introducing activities to regain confidence in balance
The patient should remain in strict bed rest indefinitely with no gradual increase in activity
The patient should immediately resume unrestricted vigorous exercise with no gradual progression
Mobility should be permanently avoided to prevent any further vertigo

stem: If hearing loss affects a patient's understanding during the subacute phase of labyrinthitis, what should the nurse facilitate?
options: Communication, using alternative communication methods
Complete cessation of all communication attempts
Exclusive use of written communication in a language the patient cannot read
Avoidance of any explanation about the patient's condition

stem: Patient and family education in the subacute phase of labyrinthitis should include teaching about which topics?
options: The condition, its causes, and the importance of adhering to prescribed treatments
Only unrelated dietary recipes with no connection to the illness
Only the hospital's visiting hours policy
Only the names of unrelated hospital staff members

stem: When educating about medications such as antibiotics or antivirals for labyrinthitis, what key adherence point should the nurse emphasize?
options: The importance of completing the full course of therapy
That the medication may be stopped as soon as symptoms improve even slightly
That doubling the dose will speed up recovery
That the medication has no possible side effects whatsoever

stem: Reinforcing vestibular rehabilitation exercises in labyrinthitis recovery serves which purpose?
options: To improve balance and reduce dizziness, as directed by the rehabilitation team
To permanently eliminate the need for any follow-up care
To replace the need for antiviral or antibiotic therapy entirely
To increase, rather than reduce, vertigo symptoms over time

stem: In long-term care for labyrinthitis, the nurse should monitor for which persistent complications?
options: Persistent hearing loss, chronic dizziness, or psychological effects such as anxiety or depression
Only unrelated changes in appetite with no connection to the ear
Only changes in handwriting legibility
Only changes in favorite leisure activities

stem: Promoting follow-up care in long-term labyrinthitis management includes encouraging regular visits to which specialists?
options: Audiologists or ENT specialists
Only a podiatrist
Only a dermatologist
Only a dentist

stem: Supporting psychosocial well-being in long-term labyrinthitis care includes providing which type of support?
options: Reassurance and emotional support, with referral to counseling services if needed
Strict isolation from family and friends to promote independence
Discouragement of any discussion about the patient's symptoms or feelings
Withholding all information about the condition from the patient

stem: Which of the following is listed as a primary NURSING GOAL in the care of a patient with labyrinthitis?
options: Preventing complications like falls and dehydration
Maximizing the patient's exposure to loud noise
Encouraging rapid, unsupervised ambulation during acute vertigo
Discontinuing all medications as soon as the patient is admitted

stem: Besides preventing falls and dehydration, which other nursing goal is identified for labyrinthitis care?
options: Promoting symptom relief and comfort, and supporting the patient in regaining independence and confidence
Ensuring the patient receives no education about coping strategies
Ensuring the patient avoids all follow-up appointments after discharge
Ensuring the patient discontinues vestibular rehabilitation exercises immediately

stem: A nursing goal of educating on coping strategies and adherence to treatment plans in labyrinthitis primarily supports which outcome?
options: Long-term recovery and prevention of complications
Immediate, permanent cure within the first hour of admission
Complete avoidance of any future medical follow-up
Replacement of medical therapy with coping strategies alone

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A 34-year-old man develops sudden severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus, two days after resolving a bout of influenza. He has no prior ear surgery and no history of recurrent episodic vertigo. Which diagnosis is MOST consistent with this presentation, and which differential should be ruled out given the hearing loss?
options: Viral labyrinthitis is most consistent, given the preceding viral illness and combined vestibular and auditory symptoms; Meniere's disease should be considered but is typically episodic and recurrent rather than a single acute event
Vestibular neuritis is most consistent, since it always presents with hearing loss identical to labyrinthitis
Acoustic neuroma is confirmed by this presentation alone, with no further imaging required
This presentation requires no further evaluation, since vertigo following influenza is never clinically significant

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient hospitalized with labyrinthitis following untreated otitis media develops worsening vertigo, high fever, and increasing unilateral hearing loss over several days despite supportive care. Which concern should the nurse prioritize, and why?
options: Concern for bacterial labyrinthitis progressing toward permanent hearing loss or vestibular dysfunction if not treated promptly, warranting urgent reassessment and likely antibiotic therapy
No concern is warranted, since all labyrinthitis resolves spontaneously regardless of cause or treatment
The nurse should discontinue all monitoring, since fever in labyrinthitis is never clinically significant
The worsening symptoms confirm a diagnosis of Meniere's disease, which requires no further intervention

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient in the acute phase of labyrinthitis attempts to walk unassisted to the bathroom during a severe vertigo episode in a dimly lit, cluttered room. Which nursing priority BEST reflects safe, evidence-based care for this patient?
options: Assist with mobility, remove obstacles, and ensure a clutter-free, safe environment to reduce the risk of falls during vertigo episodes
Encourage the patient to continue walking unassisted to promote independence regardless of fall risk
Leave the room as is, since environmental modification has no role in labyrinthitis care
Increase room lighting to maximum brightness and add background music to stimulate alertness

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient recovering from labyrinthitis reports persistent dizziness and difficulty regaining confidence in walking several weeks after the acute illness resolved, alongside low mood related to the prolonged symptoms. Which combination of interventions is MOST appropriate at this stage?
options: Vestibular rehabilitation therapy with gradually introduced activity, along with reassurance, emotional support, and referral to counseling services if distress is significant
Strict indefinite bed rest with no vestibular rehabilitation or emotional support of any kind
Immediate discontinuation of all follow-up care, since persistent dizziness after labyrinthitis is never clinically relevant
Exclusive reliance on high-dose antibiotics alone, with no rehabilitation or psychosocial component

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient with confirmed viral labyrinthitis is prescribed an antiviral agent and a short course of meclizine, and is counseled to avoid driving. Three days later the patient reports feeling much better and wants to stop all medication and resume full activity immediately. Which nursing response is MOST appropriate?
options: Reinforce the importance of completing the prescribed course of therapy and gradually, rather than abruptly, resuming activity, since recovery from viral labyrinthitis can take weeks to months even when symptoms improve early
Agree that all medication should be stopped immediately once the patient feels subjectively better
Advise the patient to double the antiviral dose to accelerate full recovery
Tell the patient that full, unrestricted activity should resume immediately, since three days of improvement guarantees complete resolution
